activities.anchor: Explained facts the standard model could not
activities.caption: pair each feature with its consequence
activities.name: bfProspectMatch

config.prompt: The measured value function — pair each feature with what it produces:

pairs.right: outcomes weighed against the purchase price, not wealth
losses loom about twice as large as equivalent gains
risk-seeking for losses, risk-averse for gains

config.why: Kahneman and Tversky (1979) replaced the rational value function with a measured one — and explained why investors hold losers, why insurers sell deductibles, why gamblers chase.

activities.anchor: The arithmetic explains portfolio behaviour the rational model calls error
activities.caption: true or false — the meter with double weight
activities.name: bfValueJudge

statements.s: Winning 100 feels like about +1 unit of value; losing 100 feels like about −2.2.
statements.why: The measured value function prices a loss at roughly twice a gain.

statements.s: A 50/50 coin flip of plus-or-minus 100 has positive subjective value.
statements.why: About −0.6 — refused; yet the same coin flipped over an existing loss is eagerly accepted.

statements.s: The shorter the evaluation horizon, the smaller the premium needed to hold stocks.
statements.why: The other way round: frequent checks deliver regular loss experiences at double weight, so a bigger premium is needed.

statements.s: Insurers selling deductibles and gamblers chasing losses trace to the same flattened value function.
statements.why: Risk-seeking in the loss domain, risk-aversion in the gain domain — facts the standard model could not explain.

activities.anchor: Calibrating the model to plausible check frequencies
activities.caption: call the magnitude — the oldest premium puzzle
activities.name: bfPremiumEstimate

config.prompt: Historically, by roughly how much a year have stocks outperformed Treasury bills (geometric)?
config.why: About 5–6% — more than any plausible risk aversion justifies (Mehra and Prescott's 1985 puzzle). Benartzi and Thaler's myopic loss aversion reproduces the observed premium from realistic checking behaviour: the rare behavioural result that solves a puzzle with numbers.

activities.caption: find the faulty line — the suitability spec
activities.name: bfSuitSpot

config.prompt: One line of this suitability questionnaire's spec is wrong — click it:
lines: People file money in non-fungible buckets: dividends feel like spending money.
The same dollar is treated differently depending on its mental ledger.
The same accounting files nominal house prices as 'wealth'.
Good suitability practice asks about stated preferences on a scale of 1 to 10.
The honest probe is behaviour in past drawdowns.
config.correction: Good suitability practice asks about behaviour in past drawdowns — stated preferences are exactly what the mental ledgers corrupt.
config.why: Cash filed as 'safe' and house prices filed as 'wealth' show how households maximise the feeling of safety while minimising its substance — measure the behaviour, not the self-image.

config.root: You are a subject in the 1981 experiment. An outbreak is expected to kill 600 people. Choose a programme.

start.text: Frame one. Programme A: 200 people will be saved for certain. Programme B: a 1/3 chance that 600 will be saved, a 2/3 chance that nobody is. Choose.

choices.label: Programme A — the certain save
choices.feedback: You are with 72% of subjects — risk-averse when the frame is lives saved.

choices.label: Programme B — the gamble
choices.feedback: You are with 28% — the minority under this frame.

frame2.text: Frame two — same outbreak, re-described. Programme C: 400 people will die for certain. Programme D: a 1/3 chance that nobody dies, a 2/3 chance that all 600 die. Choose.

choices.label: Programme C — the certain outcome
choices.feedback: Only 28% chose this — though it is Programme A, unchanged in substance.

choices.label: Programme D — gamble on the deaths
choices.feedback: 78% took the gamble — the loss frame flipped the risk appetite without moving one number.

end.text: The invariance axiom — descriptions should not matter — fails measurably.

config.why: In finance the same trade reads as 'locking in a gain' or 'missing further upside' — a screen showing unrealised losses produces different behaviour than the identical numbers shown as returns since purchase.

activities.anchor: A pricing anomaly became a preference measurement
activities.caption: drag the divider — the line the model draws vs the line the data draw
activities.name: bfBetaCompare

config.prompt: The security market line, twice — drag the divider:

before.label: CAPM says
before.text: High-beta assets earn more — the line slopes upward with beta, paying for the market risk each asset contributes.

after.label: The data say
after.text: The line comes out flat: low-beta portfolios match or beat high-beta ones after risk-adjustment. Investors pay a premium for lottery-like glamour, and leverage constraints push risk-seekers into high-beta stocks instead of borrowing.

config.why: Frazzini and Pedersen's betting-against-beta mechanism monetises the gap — a taste story, reinforced by constraints, that turned an anomaly into a preference measurement.

activities.anchor: a pattern no risk-based model wants
activities.caption: bet on the winners
activities.name: bfMomentumPredict

config.q: You screen for stocks that won over the past year and buy them. What did Jegadeesh and Titman (1993) find happens over the following months?
choices: Losers catch up — the reversal takes over
Winners keep beating losers by roughly 12% a year
config.why: About 12% a year, roughly 1% a month, replicated across international markets — and its persistence after publication, punctuated by the momentum crash of 2009, makes it the field's central test case for risk versus psychology.
